one_liner: SPARK/Ada re-implementation of TweetNaCl with proven absence of run-time errors; the author reports Ed25519 Sign about 3x faster than TweetNaCl C on a RISC-V board.
what_it_does: A re-implementation of TweetNaCl (Ed25519 signatures, X25519, Salsa20/XSalsa20 box and secretbox, Poly1305, SHA-512) in SPARK 2014. Later contributions added ChaCha20, SHA-256 and SHA-384, HMAC and HKDF, an RFC 8439 AEAD and RFSB509. It keeps TweetNaCl's API semantics and constant-time algorithms, but exposes them as Ada packages (SPARKNaCl.Sign, SPARKNaCl.Cryptobox and others) built as a GPR/Alire library. The whole library carries an automated GNATprove proof of type safety (no overflow, out-of-bounds index or uninitialised read) and runs on the zero-footprint runtime.
how_it_is_fast: The proof bounds every field-element limb (Normal_GF limbs are 0..65535), so the code can be built with -gnatp (all run-time checks off) and the arithmetic can be rewritten safely. GF(2^255-19) multiplication is a fully unrolled product-scanning multiply: each partial product is a 16x16-bit limb product in a 32-bit type (one 32-bit multiply on rv32im), the 38x reduction and the first carry pass are fused into the digit loop, and there is a dedicated Square and a hand-unrolled Inv_25519 (2023 commits). The TweetNaCl C baseline instead multiplies 64-bit limbs and then runs two separate carry passes. The gain therefore comes from different field arithmetic that the proofs made safe to write, not from Ada code generation.
when_to_use: Bare-metal or safety-critical embedded targets (zero-footprint runtime, no heap, no OS) that need Ed25519, X25519 or NaCl box/secretbox with a machine-checked proof of absence of run-time errors.
Ada or SPARK code bases that want NaCl primitives through Alire, with readable contract-annotated sources for assurance reviews.

Small 32-bit cores, especially RISC-V, where TweetNaCl is the current choice and its 64-bit-limb multiply is costly; the author's blog posts report roughly 2x to 3.5x fewer cycles for Sign (snippet-only numbers).
Certification or audit settings where proven type safety and tracked worst-case stack usage (GNATstack reported 5648 bytes for Sign on 32-bit RISC-V in 2020) matter more than peak throughput.
when_not_to_use: Server or desktop throughput on x86-64 or ARM64: there is no SIMD or assembly, and it has only ever been compared against TweetNaCl, a deliberately compact C library, never against speed-oriented C crypto libraries.
Calling from C or C++: a C API wrapper is still on the README's to-do list.
When you need reproducible published numbers: the cycle tables live only in AdaCore blog posts and slides, and the README (June 2022) says the latest '*' results are still to be documented.
-O0 builds: the README says the 2022 '*' rewrite is noticeably slower at -O0, and results swing strongly with the optimisation level.

When constant-time behaviour must be machine-checked: the README claims proof of type safety and some correctness properties; constant-time behaviour is kept by construction, not proven for the whole library.

integration.form: static lib (GPR library project or Alire crate 'sparknacl', 4.0.0 in alire.toml; static, static-pic or relocatable)
integration.dependencies: none at run time (works on the GNAT zero-footprint runtime); proving needs GNATprove ^14.1.1 with Z3, CVC5 and Alt-Ergo per sparknacl.gpr
integration.min_toolchain: GNAT >= 14.2.1 per alire.toml (release 3.0.0 supported GNAT Community 2020/2021 and FSF GNAT 11.2.1+); performance tests need a riscv64-elf GNAT cross compiler and Ada_Drivers_Library
integration.platforms: any GNAT target; performance tested on SiFive HiFive1 Rev B (FE310, 32-bit RISC-V); tests reproduced on macOS, Linux and Windows
integration.thread_safety: the packages are declared Pure (no package-level state), so calls should be reentrant; thread safety is not otherwise documented
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same NaCl/TweetNaCl functions and identical outputs (the NaCl test suite is re-implemented and passes), but as an Ada API rather than the crypto_* C API; no C wrapper yet

gotchas: Harness flag asymmetry: since commit e06da81 (2021-02-17, 'Switch to RV32IMC_A4 by default'), perf/tsign.mk sets SPARKNACL_TARGET_ARCH=rv32imc_a4. That makes sparknacl.gpr compile the SPARK library with -march=rv32imc plus -falign-functions/-jumps/-loops/-labels=4, while perf.gpr compiles perf/tweetnacl.c with -march=rv32im ('No compressed instructions for C') and no alignment flags. At -O1 and above the library also gets -gnatn cross-unit inlining. The record's 'same flags' description therefore holds only for the -O level, not the ISA or code alignment. Per a search snippet, the author had found the E31 core pays a penalty for branches to misaligned compressed code. The effect on the published Sign numbers is unknown.

Algorithm asymmetry behind the numbers: SPARKNaCl multiplies 16-bit limbs as 32-bit products with fused reduction and carry, and adds a dedicated Square. perf/tweetnacl.c (already patched with the WireGuard carry and an unrolled inner loop 'as per SPARKNaCl') still multiplies i64 limbs, a multi-instruction operation on rv32im, then runs two car25519 passes. The same rewrite is possible in C, so this is library versus library.

perf/tsign.adb times one Sign per side, single run, from code executing out of SPI flash through the instruction cache. The SPARK Sign runs right after SPARKNaCl.Sign.Keypair, which exercises the same SHA-512 and scalar-multiply code, while TweetNaCl's crypto_sign runs cold. This is probably small next to tens of millions of cycles, but it is not controlled.

Proof covers the source, not the compiled code: GNAT 14 miscompiled SHA-256 at -O2/-O3 on x86-64 (issue #37, March 2025, fixed with -fno-tree-vrp). sparknacl.gpr adds -fno-tree-vrp only when SPARKNACL_TARGET_ARCH is 'unspecified', so the rv32im, rv32imc and rv32imc_a4 builds do not get the workaround. Run the test suite at your own optimisation level.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick SPARKNaCl when you need proven-safe public-key crypto (Ed25519, X25519) on bare-metal or Ada targets. Pick tachyon-rs for AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305 or hashing throughput on desktop or mobile CPUs, and Usuba for bitsliced symmetric ciphers on SIMD hardware; neither offers a type-safety proof or a zero-footprint runtime.
verified_claims_summary: Per AdaCore blog and slide snippets only (blog.adacore.com and www.adacore.com unreachable here), one Ed25519 Sign of a 256-byte message on a HiFive1 Rev B (FE310 RISC-V, GNAT Community GCC 8/10 cross compiler, mcycle) went from SPARK roughly level with TweetNaCl at -O1 and behind at -O2 in February 2021 (93.86 vs 84.99 million cycles at -O2) to about 24.37 million cycles at -O2 after tuning, versus 84.99 million for the original TweetNaCl and 51.00 million for a C version patched with some of the same tricks. That is about 3.5x and 2.1x (derived from snippet data). The committed harness compares the two in one image and checks the signatures match, but it builds them with different -march and alignment flags.
status_note: Maintained: proof-maintenance commits in March 2026 for GNATprove updates and an SHA-384 contribution in 2025, with three open issues. It is BSD-3-Clause, small and Alire-packaged, so it is easy to adopt in Ada; performance claims rest on 2021-2022 blog posts about older code.
